o1.biggest_strength: It uses COD refusals in the decision. It adds a lip balm cart offer for orders under ₹499, proposes a ₹49 COD fee, and works out break-even for each bundle. It also gives a full test plan with stop rules and guardrails.
o1.biggest_mistake: It is dense and a bit over the word limit. The 'bad news' block and the many projection ranges make it hard to skim. It also keeps the ₹499 threshold with only a weak case, so the main money question ends in 'test it'.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Trim it to the word limit and state the threshold call more firmly, with one clear recommended number and a simpler money table. Spell out the ₹500 to 699 band maths at the top. Make the lip balm cart add-on a named fourth item instead of a side note.

o2.biggest_strength: It is clean and easy to read. The bundle ladder on the serum page is a good idea. It also commits to a clear threshold (₹599) and shows a simple outcome table.
o2.biggest_mistake: The threshold maths rests on an invented guess that only 6% of orders sit between ₹499 and ₹598. That gives a gain of only about ₹28k a month. It also barely uses COD and RTO for small orders, and it never considers a COD fee or a prepaid-only rule.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Replace the 6% guess with a figure drawn from the order bands, and build COD refusal cost into the threshold decision. Make the three bundles three different jobs by dropping the overlapping Serum + Lip Balm bundle for a body or add-on bundle. Add a cart add-on to cross the threshold.

reason: The first one deals with the COD refusal leak, uses the lip balm as the add-on, and gives three bundles with distinct jobs and worked break-evens. The second is neater but its threshold case rests on a guessed slice of orders, it overlaps two bundles, and it mostly ignores COD.
